'''Abram Samoilovitch Besicovitch''' (or '''Besikovitch''';<ref name="frs">{{Cite journal | last1 = Burkill | first1 = J. C. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.1971.0001  | doi-access = free| title = Abram Samoilovitch Besicovitch 1891-1970 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 17 | pages = 1–16| year = 1971 }}</ref> {{langx|ru|link=no|Абра́м Само́йлович Безико́вич}}; 23 January 1891 – 2 November 1970) was a [[Russian Empire|Russia]]n [[mathematician]]. He was professor at [[Cambridge University]] and worked mainly in [[mathematical analysis|analysis]].

==Life and career==
Abram Besicovitch was born in [[Berdyansk]] on the [[Sea of Azov]] (now in [[Ukraine]]) to a [[Karaite Judaism|Karaite]] Jewish family.<ref>{{cite journal|title=On generalized almost periodic functions|journal=Proc. London Math. Soc.|volume=25|issue=2|year=1926|pages=495–512|doi=10.1112/plms/s2-25.1.495|last1=Besicovitch|first1=A. S.}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Tamarkin, J. D.|author-link=Jacob Tamarkin|title=Besicovitch on Almost Periodic Functions|journal=Bull. Am. Math. Soc.|year=1935|volume=41|issue=7|pages=461–462|url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bams/1183498280|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1935-06112-9|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=The Kakeya Problem|journal=American Mathematical Monthly|volume=70|year=1963|pages=697–706|mr=0157266|doi=10.2307/2312249|jstor=2312249|last1=Besicovitch|first1=A. S.|issue=7}}</ref><ref name="mactutor">{{MacTutor Biography|id=Besicovitch}}</ref><ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120711035033/http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/dms/load/img/?IDDOC=10655|title=Besicovitch ''On Kakeyas Problem and a similar one'', Math. Zeitschrift vol.27, 1928, 312}}</ref><ref>[http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/dms/load/img/?IDDOC=38403 Besicovitch ''On linear sets of points of fractal dimension'', Math. Annalen 1929], [http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/dms/load/img/?IDDOC=37902 Teil 2] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160107094909/http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/dms/load/img/?IDDOC=37902 |date=7 January 2016 }},</ref> He studied under the supervision of [[Andrey Markov]] at the [[Saint Petersburg State University|Saint Petersburg Imperial University]], graduating with a PhD in 1912,<ref name="mathgene"/> and then began research in [[probability theory]]. He converted to [[Eastern Orthodoxy]], joining the [[Russian Orthodox Church]], on marrying in 1916. Besicovitch was appointed professor at the [[Perm State University|University of Perm]] in 1917, and was caught up in the [[Russian Civil War]] over the next two years. In 1920, he took a position at his alma mater, now renamed the [[Saint Petersburg State University|Petrograd State University]].

In 1924, he went to [[Copenhagen]] on a [[Rockefeller Fellowship]], where he worked on [[almost periodic function]]s under [[Harald Bohr]]. A type of function space in that field now bears his name. After a visit to [[G.H. Hardy]] at the [[University of Oxford]], he had appointments at the [[University of Liverpool]] in 1926, and the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1927.

Besicovitch moved to Cambridge University in 1927, where he was made a Fellow of [[Trinity College, Cambridge|Trinity College]]. He was appointed Lecturer in the Faculty of Mathematics, and therefore received recognition as a Cambridge MA by 'Special Grace' on 24 November 1928. In 1950, he became [[John Edensor Littlewood|J.E. Littlewood's]] successor as the [[Rouse Ball Chair of Mathematics]]. He retired in 1958 and toured the US for eight years. After returning to Trinity, he died in 1970 in Cambridge. 

== Work ==
Besicovitch worked mainly on [[combinatorial methods]] and questions in [[real analysis]], such as the [[Kakeya needle problem]] and the [[Hausdorff–Besicovitch dimension]], two areas that have grown in importance in recent years. The [[Kovner–Besicovitch measure]] of the central symmetry of planar convex sets is also named after him.

He was also a major influence on the economist [[Piero Sraffa]], after 1940, when they were both Fellows of Trinity, and on [[Dennis Lindley]], one of the founders of the [[Bayesian inference|Bayesian]] movement in the United Kingdom. 

==Awards and honours==
Besicovitch was in 1934 made [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]<ref name="frs"/> and in 1952 won the [[Sylvester Medal]] from the [[Royal Society]].<ref>[http://royalsociety.org/Content.aspx?id=3372 Entry in Archive of the Royal Society].</ref> He received in 1950 the ''[[De Morgan Medal]]'' of the [[London Mathematical Society]]. He was a visiting scholar at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in the fall of 1954.<ref>[http://www.ias.edu/people/cos/ Institute for Advanced Study: A Community of Scholars]</ref>

Besicovitch's candidacy for the Royal Society reads:{{blockquote|text="''Distinguished as a pure mathematician, particularly for his researches in the theory of functions of a real variable, the theory of analytic functions, and the theory of almost periodic functions.''"<ref name="royal">{{cite web|url=http://royalsociety.org/DServe/dserve.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=(RefNo==%27EC%2F1934%2F01%27)|title = Library and Archive Catalogue|publisher=The Royal Society|access-date=13 November 2013|location=London}}</ref>}}

The asteroid ''[[16953 Besicovitch]]'' is named in his honour.

A portrait of Besicovitch by [[Eve Goldsmith Coxeter]] is in the collection of [[Trinity College, Cambridge]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Trinity College, University of Cambridge|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/arts/yourpaintings/paintings/search/located_at/trinity-college-cambridge-5846_locations|publisher=BBC Your Paintings|access-date=12 February 2018|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140511164255/http://www.bbc.co.uk/arts/yourpaintings/paintings/search/located_at/trinity-college-cambridge-5846_locations|archive-date=11 May 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Quotation==
* ''A mathematician's reputation rests on the number of bad proofs he has given.''<ref>Besicovitch, quoted in [[John Edensor Littlewood]], ''A mathematician's miscellany'', Methuen 1953, p.42. In Littlewood's words ''Pioneer work is clumsy.''</ref>
